title: Moi Moi in Leaves
author: Florence Madu
desc: A party-sized moi moi — 750 g of beans, two litres of water, twelve parcels at 420 g each — with the knife test that tells you when it is set.
longDesc: This is the version to make when you are feeding a crowd, and it is the one with the best doneness test in any Nigerian bean recipe: put a knife through it, and if it comes out stained with paste it is not ready, while a slight smear means it is. Three hours before cooking you soak and wash the beans to get the coats off. Everything then goes into the blender together — beans, tomato puree, onions, crayfish, habanero and nutmeg — and the remaining water is added slowly while stirring. The water in the pot is padded to a maximum of one inch.
ingredients: 750 g beans, brown or black-eyed (also given as three cigar cups)
800 g watery tomato puree, or 3 tatashe peppers
Hard-boiled eggs, bone marrow, or corned beef
equipment: Uma leaves, banana leaves, foil bags or bowls
steps: About three hours before cooking the moi moi, soak and wash the beans to remove the coat.
Blend the soaked beans with the tomato puree, onions, crayfish, habanero and nutmeg, using some of the water.
Pour into a bowl. Add the vegetable oil, and the bone marrow stock if you are using it.
Slowly add the remaining water while stirring.
Pad the base of the pot with water, to a maximum depth of 1 inch, and set it on the stove.
Dish the mixture into your containers, adding the meat or eggs, seal them, and place them in the pot.
Cook a minimum of 1 hour before checking.
Test by putting a knife through it. If the knife is stained with moi moi paste it is not done; if it just has a slight smear, it is done.
chefTips: The knife test is the clearest doneness cue in any Nigerian bean recipe. Stained means raw, slight smear means set.
One inch of water in the base, maximum. More and you are boiling rather than steaming.
Three hours of soaking is for the coats, not for softening. The beans need to swell enough that the skins slip.
The water goes in slowly, while stirring, after the blend. Dumped in at once it will not emulsify with the oil.
Uma or banana leaves cook fastest, then foil bags, then aluminium or plastic plates, which take the longest. Same batter, different timings.
Twelve aluminium bags at 420 g each is the stated yield — useful if you are scaling for a party.
For small quantities on high heat, 45 minutes is enough. The hour is for a full pot.
commonMistakes: Too much water in the base of the pot.
Checking before the hour is up and losing the steam.
Adding the two litres all at once.
Mixing vessel types in one pot, so some set and some do not.
Skipping the knife test and going by time alone.
sources: Adapted from 'Nigerian Moi Moi', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Local names given there: Moin Moin, Moyin Moyin, Steamed Beans Pudding. Quantities as printed: 750g beans (brown/black eyed), 5 tablespoons ground crayfish, 4 big stock cubes, 1 habanero pepper, 2 teaspoons ground nutmeg, 800g watery tomato puree or 3 tatashe peppers, 2 big onions, 20cl vegetable oil, 2 litres cool/warm water, salt to taste. The bean quantity is also given as 'three cigar cups/750g'.

THE DONENESS TEST, verbatim: 'Confirm that it is done by putting a knife through it, if the knife is stained with Moi Moi paste, then the Moi Moi is not done, but if the knife just has a slight smear of Moi Moi, then it's done.'

THE WRAPPING-VERSUS-TIME NOTE, verbatim: 'The Moi Moi that gets done quickest is the one wrapped in Uma or Banana leaves, followed by Moi Moi wrapped in aluminum foils then the one that takes the most time is Moi Moi cooked in aluminium or plastic plates.'
YIELD as printed: 12 aluminium bags at 420g each; also 45 minutes for small quantities on high heat. Uma leaf is identified on the page as Thaumatococcus Daniellii.
The three-hour soak and the 'maximum 1 inch' of padding water are both as printed. No list/method discrepancies were found on this page.

NOTE this page's treatment of tatashe: '800g watery tomato puree or 3 tatashe peppers' makes the two interchangeable, which implies a large, fleshy, mild, juicy red pepper — the red bell reading rather than the poblano one. See NGA019 for the full dispute.
DISAGREEMENT on technique with NGA022: everything is blended together in one go here, with no separate aeration step, where Sisi Jemimah beats the batter for 8 minutes and then 5 minutes more.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 2 months frozen in the wrapping.
reheating: Steam 10 to 15 minutes, or microwave in the leaf.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas supply plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Nutmeg and crayfish season it with very little added salt.
culturalNote: Moi moi at this scale is party cooking, and the twelve-parcel yield is not an accident — it is the unit a Nigerian kitchen thinks in when there is an event. The site's own framing calls it a 'dish accessory': it almost never appears alone, but alongside jollof, fried rice, dodo, custard or pap, which is why nearly every Nigerian celebration plate has a square of it somewhere on the edge.
